course.title: Node.js and Express API Development
course.subtitle: Build maintainable, secure HTTP services with Node.js, Express and reliable database practices.
course.description: An intermediate practical course covering the Node.js runtime, asynchronous JavaScript, modules, configuration, Express routing and middleware, validation, authentication, authorization, database transactions, testing, uploads, rate limiting and deployment. Learners finish with a documented course API.

Frontend developers moving into API development

sections.description: Understand the Node runtime, modules, configuration and asynchronous execution.

lessons.title: Node.js Runtime and Event Loop
lessons.body_markdown:
## Node.js Runtime and Event Loop

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser using the V8 engine and a set of runtime APIs. Its event loop coordinates callbacks and asynchronous work so a process can handle many I/O operations without creating one operating-system thread for every request.

### Worked application example

A service can read a course record from a database while other requests continue to be accepted. File access, network calls and timers often complete asynchronously, while CPU-heavy synchronous work can block the event loop.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume asynchronous means parallel CPU execution. A long synchronous loop can delay every request in the process. Keep request handlers short and move heavy workloads to a worker or job system when justified.

### Practice task

Explain the event loop using a request that reads a file and then queries a database. Identify which work blocks the main thread.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.
lessons.exercise: Explain the event loop using a request that reads a file and then queries a database. Identify which work blocks the main thread.
key_takeaways: Keep HTTP handling separate from domain rules and persistence.
Validate and authorize every request on the server.
Use database constraints, tests and observability to protect production behaviour.

lessons.title: Modules, npm and Project Configuration
lessons.body_markdown:
## Modules, npm and Project Configuration

Node applications use modules to organise code. CommonJS uses `require` and `module.exports`; ECMAScript modules use `import` and `export`. A project should choose and configure its module system deliberately, keep dependencies declared and commit a lockfile for reproducible installation.

### Worked application example

A small API can separate `server.js`, route modules, validation schemas and database access. `package.json` defines scripts and dependencies; the lockfile records resolved versions so a teammate and CI install consistent packages.

### Common failure to avoid

Mixing module systems without understanding package configuration causes confusing import errors. Do not install packages globally as a substitute for declaring project dependencies. Review package scripts before running unfamiliar commands.

### Practice task

Create a minimal Node project with a start script, one module export and a test script. Explain the purpose of package.json and the lockfile.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Environment Variables and Configuration
lessons.body_markdown:
## Environment Variables and Configuration

Configuration varies between local development, testing and production. Environment variables keep deployment-specific values out of source code, but they are not automatically secret merely because they are variables. Validate required configuration at startup and fail clearly when a mandatory value is absent.

### Worked application example

An API may need a database URL, a session secret and a port. Load local variables with an approved development setup, validate their presence and pass them to the modules that need them rather than reading process.env everywhere.

### Common failure to avoid

Never commit credentials or expose server secrets in API responses or browser bundles. Do not silently fall back to a production credential when local configuration is missing.

### Practice task

Design a configuration module that validates a database URL and session secret. Describe how you would rotate a leaked secret.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript and Promises
lessons.body_markdown:
## Asynchronous JavaScript and Promises

Promises represent work that may finish later. `async` functions return promises, and `await` pauses that function until a promise settles without blocking the entire Node process. Use `try/catch` for expected failure handling and preserve useful error context.

### Worked application example

A route may await a database lookup and return a response when the query completes. Two independent lookups can run with Promise.all; dependent operations must remain ordered so a write does not occur before a required permission check.

### Common failure to avoid

An unhandled rejected promise can create unstable behaviour. Do not start asynchronous work and forget to await or handle it. Do not run independent tasks sequentially unless their results depend on each other.

### Practice task

Rewrite a callback-based file read as an async function. Include missing-file and permission-error handling.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: HTTP Fundamentals and Express Application
lessons.body_markdown:
## HTTP Fundamentals and Express Application

Express is a web framework that maps HTTP requests to middleware and route handlers. An application receives a method, path, headers and possibly a body, then returns a status, headers and response. Understand HTTP before treating Express as magic.

### Worked application example

A GET `/api/courses` route can return public course summaries. A POST `/api/enrolments` route can accept an enrolment request, validate it and return a created or conflict response.

### Common failure to avoid

A route that always returns 200 hides failures from clients and monitoring. Use correct methods and status codes, and never trust the request body just because JSON parsing succeeded.

### Practice task

Design three routes for a course API and specify method, path, input, response and likely error statuses.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Express Middleware and Request Lifecycle
lessons.body_markdown:
## Express Middleware and Request Lifecycle

Middleware functions run during the request-response lifecycle. They can parse bodies, attach request context, authenticate a caller, log safe metadata or handle errors. Middleware order matters because each function may pass control onward, end the response or raise an error.

### Worked application example

A request can pass through JSON parsing, request ID assignment, authentication, route validation and a final error handler. Public catalogue routes may not require learner authentication, while protected lesson routes do.

### Common failure to avoid

Middleware that neither responds nor calls next leaves the request hanging. Authentication middleware should not accidentally protect public routes or trust a role sent by the client.

### Practice task

Draw the middleware order for public and protected API routes. Identify where errors should be forwarded and handled.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.
lessons.exercise: Draw the middleware order for public and protected API routes. Identify where errors should be forwarded and handled.

lessons.title: Routing, Controllers and Domain Services
lessons.body_markdown:
## Routing, Controllers and Domain Services

Keep route declarations, HTTP translation and business rules separate. A controller interprets the request and response; a domain service enforces application rules; a repository or data-access module handles persistence. This separation makes business logic easier to test without an HTTP server.

### Worked application example

An enrolment controller can validate the incoming course ID, call an enrolment service and translate outcomes into 201, 409 or 404. The service checks course publication and duplicate enrolment before saving.

### Common failure to avoid

Putting SQL, authorization, validation and response formatting in one giant route makes changes risky. Do not duplicate the same business rule across multiple controllers.

### Practice task

Refactor a single route into controller, service and repository layers. Write a unit test for the service without starting Express.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Validation, Errors and API Responses
lessons.body_markdown:
## Validation, Errors and API Responses

Treat all incoming data as untrusted. Validate shape, type, range, length and allowed values before domain logic. Return consistent error structures and avoid leaking stack traces, SQL messages or internal paths to clients.

### Worked application example

A progress endpoint may accept a lesson ID and a position between zero and the lesson duration. Reject negative values, oversized payloads and unknown identifiers before writing to the database.

### Common failure to avoid

Client-side validation is only a usability feature. An attacker can call the API directly. Do not use broad catch blocks that turn every failure into a successful empty response.

### Practice task

Create a validation schema for a course creation request. Include missing fields, excessive title length and invalid price cases.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Authentication and Session Security
lessons.body_markdown:
## Authentication and Session Security

Authentication establishes the caller's identity. Session management maintains that identity across requests. Use established libraries or managed identity providers rather than inventing password storage and token cryptography. Store password hashes, not plaintext passwords, and use secure cookie settings for browser sessions.

### Worked application example

A protected route can read a signed session from an HttpOnly, Secure and appropriately SameSite cookie, then resolve the user on the server. The browser should not be able to read an HttpOnly session cookie through JavaScript.

### Common failure to avoid

A valid token does not prove the caller owns every record. Do not store long-lived secrets in localStorage without understanding the threat model, and never log session tokens.

### Practice task

Describe a sign-in flow from credential submission to session validation. Identify cookie attributes and the server-side ownership check.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Authorization, Roles and Database Security
lessons.body_markdown:
## Authorization, Roles and Database Security

Authorization evaluates whether an authenticated user may perform a specific action on a resource. Roles can describe broad capabilities, but ownership and resource state often matter too. Enforce important restrictions in the service and database, not only in route visibility.

### Worked application example

A learner can read their own progress and enrolled lessons. An instructor may manage assigned course content. A content reviewer may approve a version but should not approve their own work if policy forbids it.

### Common failure to avoid

Never trust a `role` field in the request body. A service-role database credential can bypass row-level security, so use it only in tightly controlled server code with explicit authorization.

### Practice task

Create a role-permission matrix for learner, instructor and reviewer. Add one ownership rule that a role alone cannot express.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Database Access and Transactions
lessons.body_markdown:
## Database Access and Transactions

Database operations should use parameterised queries or a well-designed data client. Transactions keep related writes consistent: either all required changes commit or none do. Use database constraints to protect invariants against concurrent requests.

### Worked application example

Free enrolment might insert an enrolment row only when the course is published and the learner has no existing active enrolment. A unique constraint can prevent duplicates even if two requests arrive at nearly the same time.

### Common failure to avoid

Checking for a duplicate in application code and then inserting without a database constraint creates a race condition. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

### Practice task

Design a transaction for enrolling a learner and recording an audit event. State which constraints and rollback behaviour are required.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Testing Node and Express Services
lessons.body_markdown:
## Testing Node and Express Services

Unit tests check pure functions and domain services. Integration tests verify routes, middleware and database interactions. End-to-end tests validate the real user journey. Use isolated test data and ensure tests clean up after themselves.

### Worked application example

Test a course route with a valid request, malformed body, unauthenticated caller, unauthorized learner, missing course and database failure. Verify both the HTTP status and response shape.

### Common failure to avoid

A test suite that only mocks every database call cannot prove database constraints or row-level security. Avoid shared mutable fixtures that make tests order-dependent.

### Practice task

Write a test matrix for an enrolment endpoint with happy path, duplicate retry, invalid input and unauthorized access.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: File Uploads and External Services
lessons.body_markdown:
## File Uploads and External Services

File uploads introduce size, type, storage and malware risks. Validate file metadata on the server, use private storage for restricted materials and issue short-lived signed access where appropriate. External service calls need timeouts and failure handling.

### Worked application example

A course material upload can check the authenticated editor role, enforce a size limit, allow only expected document types and store the object under a course-version-specific path.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not trust a filename extension or browser-supplied MIME type as proof of file safety. Avoid storing large binary content directly in ordinary application rows without a deliberate reason.

### Practice task

Design a secure upload flow for a PDF lesson resource, including authorization, limits, storage policy and download access.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Rate Limits, Logging and Operational Safety
lessons.body_markdown:
## Rate Limits, Logging and Operational Safety

Rate limiting reduces abuse and protects expensive endpoints. Logs help diagnose failures, but should contain request IDs, operation names and safe metadata rather than credentials or sensitive content. Health checks should report service readiness without exposing secrets.

### Worked application example

A sign-in endpoint may have per-IP and per-account limits. A progress endpoint may accept repeated idempotent updates but should still have payload and request limits.

### Common failure to avoid

Rate limits must account for shared networks and legitimate retries. Logging an Authorization header or full request body can turn observability into a data breach.

### Practice task

Propose rate limits and structured log fields for sign-in, course search and file upload. List fields that must never be logged.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Deployment and Graceful Shutdown
lessons.body_markdown:
## Deployment and Graceful Shutdown

A production Node service needs a repeatable build, configuration validation, health checks and controlled shutdown. On shutdown, stop accepting new requests, allow in-flight work to finish within a deadline and close database connections. Deployments should be observable and reversible.

### Worked application example

A container or managed host can start the API with a defined command, expose a health endpoint and receive a termination signal during release. The server should close its database pool before exiting.

### Common failure to avoid

A process that works on a developer laptop may fail in production because of missing variables, wrong start scripts or assumptions about writable local storage. Do not store durable uploads on ephemeral disk.

### Practice task

Write a deployment checklist with environment validation, health check, migration plan, shutdown behaviour and rollback criteria.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build a Course API
lessons.body_markdown:
## Capstone: Build a Course API

Build an Express API that lists published courses, returns course details, accepts free enrolment, serves protected lesson metadata and records learner progress. Separate routes, controllers, services and data access. Document the API and use a consistent error format.

### Worked application example

The enrolment flow derives the learner from a verified session, checks publication and duplicate state, then writes safely. Lesson access verifies active enrolment in the exact course version. Progress updates are bounded and idempotent.

### Common failure to avoid

A route hidden in the UI is still callable. The capstone is not secure until direct requests from an unauthenticated user and a different learner are denied. Keep privileged credentials server-only and use database constraints.

### Practice task

Submit source code, route documentation, schema or data model, tests, security matrix, setup instructions and deployment checklist.

### Verification

Test the normal request and at least one invalid or unauthorized request. Record the expected HTTP status, response shape and whether a database write should occur. Explain what evidence would show that the behaviour is correct rather than merely appearing correct in the browser.
